list.name: Deploys (first start of version)
list.textFormat: {{deployment.environment.name}}. Earliest retained process start for this version (90d history). Rollbacks to a retained version do not add a deploy dot.

list.name: Process starts
list.textFormat: {{deployment.environment.name}} · {{service.version}} · {{service.instance.id}} · pod {{k8s.pod.uid}}. Includes rollout, restart and scale-up; telemetry cannot distinguish their cause.

description: The workflow engine's altinn.workflow_engine.* OpenTelemetry metrics and warning and error logs: the first screen (right now: health, processes, missing engines, unresolved failed, active and scheduled workflows; in the time range: failures, engine errors, retries and the workflows that ended), where to look (each service owner's engine, each app's workflows right now, unresolved failed workflows over time and failures by app with their traces, engine errors and logs), workflow lifecycle, latency, resources, mailboxes and throttling. Right now means the samples of the last minute before the end of the time range. A counter that never fired reads 0; No data means no engine reported, except where a latency panel says what was not measured. In the log panels an empty panel means no such records. Resource Utilization, Engine Internals, Mailboxes and Lease & Recovery Signals are collapsed; open a row to load its panels.

panels.description: The engines' own assessment of their health right now (at the end of the time range), the worst of all selected service owners' engine processes: Healthy, or Degraded while an engine's queue is full or it cannot reach its database. No data means no engine process reported in the last minute; see Processes. Service Owners below shows which engine and why.
panels.title: Engine Health

panels.description: Engine processes that sent telemetry in the minute before the end of the time range, all selected service owners together. Localtest runs one. This counts processes that send telemetry, not Kubernetes readiness. No data means no engine process is reporting.
panels.title: Processes
Unresolved Failed
panels.description: Workflows that ended failed or dependency-failed and that nobody has dealt with yet, right now (at the end of the time range): the workflows in status Failed or DependencyFailed, which each engine counts per app in its database every 15 seconds. Canceled workflows are left out: a cancellation is deliberate. A workflow leaves the count when it is resumed or abandoned, when a dependency-failed workflow's dependency succeeds after all, or when retention deletes it, by default 90 days after it was last updated, so the count ignores the time range and can hold failures from long before it. An engine that does not report per-app counts yet is counted with its canceled workflows included. Added up over the selected service owners. Every engine process of a service owner reads the same count from that service owner's database, so each service owner is counted once, not once per process. It covers only the engines reporting now: the workflows of an engine that stopped reporting drop out though they are still in its database; Missing Engines and Processes show such an engine. While an engine cannot reach its database it keeps reporting the last counts it read. Unresolved Failed over Time below shows it per service owner, Workflows by App Right Now per app. Select the number to see it by service owner or by app.

targets.expr: sum((sum by ("deployment.environment.name", "altinn.service_owner") (max by ("deployment.environment.name", "altinn.service_owner", "service.name", "altinn.workflow_engine.namespace", "altinn.workflow_engine.workflow.status") (last_over_time({"altinn.workflow_engine.workflow.count", "deployment.environment.name"=~"$env", "service.name"=~"$service", "altinn.service_owner"=~"$service_owner", "altinn.workflow_engine.workflow.status"=~"^(failed|dependency_failed)$"}[1m]))) or sum by ("deployment.environment.name", "altinn.service_owner") (max by ("deployment.environment.name", "altinn.service_owner", "service.name") (last_over_time({"altinn.workflow_engine.workflow.failed", "deployment.environment.name"=~"$env", "service.name"=~"$service", "altinn.service_owner"=~"$service_owner"}[1m])))))

panels.title: Active
panels.description: Workflows that have not finished, right now (at the end of the time range): enqueued, processing, requeued, waiting or held, counted in each engine's database. It includes the Scheduled ones, so do not add the two. Added up over the selected service owners. Every engine process of a service owner reads the same count from that service owner's database, so each service owner is counted once, not once per process. Select the number to see it by service owner.

panels.title: Scheduled
panels.description: Workflows set to start at a later time, right now (at the end of the time range), counted in each engine's database. They are also counted in Active. Added up over the selected service owners. Every engine process of a service owner reads the same count from that service owner's database, so each service owner is counted once, not once per process. Select the number to see it by service owner.

panels.title: Failed
panels.description: Workflow failures in the selected time range, from the engine's failure counter, for every reason: a step failed, a step's wait budget ran out, a dependency failed, the workflow was poisoned, or someone failed it by hand. It counts failures, not workflows: a workflow that is resumed and fails again counts twice. Canceled workflows are not counted. Added up over the selected service owners and over their engine processes, each of which counts the workflows it ran. 0 when none failed; No data when no engine reported in the time range. Select the number to see them by app.

panels.title: Engine Errors
panels.description: Exceptions in the engine's own loops in the selected time range (fetching work, database maintenance, counting workflows, the throttle and mailbox sweeps, a workflow's handling outside its steps), added up over the selected service owners and their engine processes. These are not failed workflows. 0 when there were none; No data when no engine reported in the time range. Select the number for the log records behind it or the errors by operation.

panels.title: Retries
panels.description: Retries in the selected time range: every retry of a failed step, plus every workflow put back in the queue because its engine process shut down. Added up over the selected service owners and their engine processes. Steps with a retry strategy retry as designed; a rise means some step keeps failing. 0 when nothing was retried; No data when no engine reported in the time range.

targets.expr: ((sum(increase_pure({"altinn.workflow_engine.step.execution.requeued", "deployment.environment.name"=~"$env", "service.name"=~"$service", "altinn.service_owner"=~"$service_owner"}[$__range])) or vector(0)) + (sum(increase_pure({"altinn.workflow_engine.workflow.execution.requeued", "deployment.environment.name"=~"$env", "service.name"=~"$service", "altinn.service_owner"=~"$service_owner", "altinn.workflow_engine.reason"="shutdown"}[$__range])) or vector(0))) and on () max(max_over_time({"altinn.workflow_engine.health.status", "deployment.environment.name"=~"$env", "service.name"=~"$service", "altinn.service_owner"=~"$service_owner"}[$__range]))

panels.title: Succeeded
panels.description: Workflows that finished successfully in the selected time range, added up over the selected service owners and their engine processes. 0 when none did; No data when no engine reported in the time range.

panels.title: Success Rate
panels.description: Of the workflows that ended in the selected time range, the share that succeeded: succeeded ÷ (succeeded + failed + canceled), over all selected service owners and their engine processes. None ended when no workflow ended in the time range; No data when no engine reported in it.

targets.expr: (100 * (sum(increase_pure({"altinn.workflow_engine.workflow.execution.success", "deployment.environment.name"=~"$env", "service.name"=~"$service", "altinn.service_owner"=~"$service_owner"}[$__range])) or vector(0)) / (((sum(increase_pure({"altinn.workflow_engine.workflow.execution.success", "deployment.environment.name"=~"$env", "service.name"=~"$service", "altinn.service_owner"=~"$service_owner"}[$__range])) or vector(0)) + (sum(increase_pure({"altinn.workflow_engine.workflow.execution.failed", "deployment.environment.name"=~"$env", "service.name"=~"$service", "altinn.service_owner"=~"$service_owner"}[$__range])) or vector(0)) + (sum(increase_pure({"altinn.workflow_engine.workflow.execution.canceled", "deployment.environment.name"=~"$env", "service.name"=~"$service", "altinn.service_owner"=~"$service_owner"}[$__range])) or vector(0))) > 0)) or (0 * max(max_over_time({"altinn.workflow_engine.health.status", "deployment.environment.name"=~"$env", "service.name"=~"$service", "altinn.service_owner"=~"$service_owner"}[$__range])) - 1)

panels.title: P95 Duration
panels.description: 95 % of the workflow attempts that ended in the selected time range took at most this long, from being queued to the end of the attempt (waiting in the queue plus processing). A retry is a separate attempt. Over all selected service owners and their engine processes. A resumed workflow's attempt is timed from the workflow's creation, so resuming old failures raises it. None ended when no attempt ended in the time range; No data when no engine reported in it.

One row per service owner's engine, in this order: degraded now, the most failures in the time range, the most unresolved failed, degraded earlier in the time range. Right now (the last minute): Health and Why, the engine's own assessment, Why being queue_full (active workflows reached the backpressure threshold, so new ones are refused with 429) or database_unavailable; Processes, the engine processes sending telemetry; Unresolved failed, the Unresolved Failed tile's count; Version (service.version); Active, which includes Scheduled; Waiting; Queue fill; and Breakers, the namespace circuit breakers tripped. During a database outage the counts and a queue_full in Why keep the values read before it. In the time range: Failed in range, which counts failures, so a workflow that fails twice counts twice; Engine errors, see Engine Errors by Operation; and Worst health. Select a service owner to show only that service owner on the whole dashboard, or its Engine errors for the log records behind the number: those whose event_name is a counted error, or every warning and error record if the logs carry no event_name.

panels.title: Workflows by App Right Now
panels.description: Per app, right now (at the end of the time range): Active, the workflows that have not finished, Scheduled and Waiting included; Scheduled; Waiting; and Unresolved failed, the Unresolved Failed tile's count. Only the apps that hold active or unresolved failed workflows, the most unresolved failed first, then the most active; when no app does, one row says so. Each engine counts per app every 15 seconds and the tiles' Active and Scheduled every 5, so they can differ for a moment. The apps of an engine that is not reporting are not listed; Missing Engines and Processes show such an engine. An engine that does not report per-app counts yet has one row, "all apps, not counted per app", with its database-wide counts, canceled workflows included. An engine names at most 1,000 apps and counts the rest together, as "other apps, counted together". Failures by App in the Selected Time Range has the failures of the time range instead.

panels.title: Engine Errors by Operation
panels.description: Exceptions in the engine's own loops per interval, by the operation that failed, added up over the selected service owners and their engine processes. These are not failed workflows (see Failed); each comes with a log record, in Engine Error Logs below. workflow_handling: running a workflow ended in an exception outside its steps' own error handling; the workflow is picked up again once its lease runs out. fetch_and_lock: the main loop could not fetch the next workflows from the database, usually because the database is unreachable. db_maintenance: the periodic database maintenance failed (retention, failing poisoned workflows, reclaiming stale ones, releasing workflows whose dependencies finished); the dashed line (right axis) is how many times in a row it has failed, on the worst process. metrics_collector: counting the workflows in the database failed, all of them or per app, so Active, Scheduled, Unresolved Failed, the apps table and the table's Queue fill and Why keep their last values. throttle_sweep: the namespace circuit breaker's periodic sweep failed. mailbox_deadline_sweep: looking for mailboxes past their deadline failed. mailbox_deadline_close: closing one mailbox past its deadline failed; the next sweep tries again. A flat line at 0 means no errors in the time range.

panels.title: Workflow Inventory

panels.description: Rate of durable yields. A deferral is a command reporting “ran fine, the awaited outcome is not available yet” — it is not a failure and does not consume a retry. Step deferrals exceed workflow deferrals whenever one workflow parks repeatedly. Wait Budget Expired is the failure mode this row is here to make visible: a step that kept deferring until its waitBudget ran out, failed with reason=wait_expired — deliberately excluded from the default ops alert, so this is where it surfaces. Nothing counted is a line at 0 where the engines report but have counted nothing here yet.
panels.title: Deferrals

panels.description: Workflows currently parked in Waiting because a step deferred. Waiting is in the Incomplete/active set — no lease, no worker slot, no backoff timer of its own — so this population is invisible in the Active/Scheduled gauges on the Workflow Inventory panel. A level that only ever rises means deferring commands are never resolving. Every replica reports the same database-wide count, so replicas are combined with max() rather than sum().
panels.title: Waiting Workflows

panels.description: Percentiles of the wait budget a deferring step actually consumed, from its first deferral to the moment it resolved — completed, expired, or failed. Recorded once per deferring step, so a step that deferred forty times contributes one sample. Compare the upper percentiles against the configured command.waitBudget (default 24h): this is the only signal that shows budgets being approached rather than blown. "No step was deferred in the time range" is shown both when the engines measured nothing here and when no engine reported.

defaults.noValue: No step was deferred in the time range

panels.title: Wait Budget Consumed (per deferring step)

panels.description: Namespace circuit breakers currently in the Tripped state. Zero is the normal reading. The gauge carries no namespace label — it is a per-process scalar — and every replica reports its own snapshot of the same shared state table, so replicas are combined with max() rather than sum(). The feature ships dark: with EngineSettings:Throttling:Enabled left false the sweep never runs and this stays flat at zero. workflow-engine-app turns it on; the engine's own test host only does with the playground compose override.
panels.title: Breakers Tripped

panels.description: Circuit-breaker state changes in the last 5 minutes, per namespace. These are rare discrete events, so this is a count over the window rather than a per-second rate like the throughput panels — one trip reads as 1, not as 0.003/s, including the first trip in a namespace, which starts a new series. Tripped includes re-trips from a failed recovery. Extended means every canary failed its probe and the throttle window doubled. Cleared means recovery drained the parked population. Handler Parked counts workflows the handler parked the moment they failed retryably in an already-tripped namespace — the sweep's own parking is not counted there, so this series stays flat when the storm is not producing fresh failures. Nothing counted is a line at 0 where the engines report but have counted nothing here yet.
panels.title: Breaker Transitions by Namespace

panels.description: Rate at which recovery cohorts hand parked workflows back to the fetch gate, per namespace. Counted by the number of rows actually released, not once per cohort, and cohorts double every sweep — so a healthy recovery is a rising curve that stops abruptly when the last cohort comes back empty and the breaker clears. This is the only throttle counter with a population large enough to read as a rate. Nothing counted is a line at 0 where the engines report but have counted nothing here yet.
panels.title: Workflows Released from Throttling by Namespace

panels.description: Workflow duration percentiles for a single attempt (queue + processing). Retries land as separate samples; see Outcomes for retry rate. "No workflow attempt ended in the time range" is shown both when the engines measured nothing here and when no engine reported.

defaults.noValue: No workflow attempt ended in the time range

panels.title: Workflow Duration (per attempt)

panels.description: Per-attempt P95 of queue wait and active execution, stacked. Stack height is the sum of two marginal P95s — useful for seeing where tail latency is concentrated, but it does not reconcile arithmetically with the Workflow Duration panel's P95(total) because percentiles are not additive across the queue/processing decomposition. Within a single attempt, queue + processing does equal total by construction. "No workflow attempt ended in the time range" is shown both when the engines measured nothing here and when no engine reported.

defaults.noValue: No workflow attempt ended in the time range

panels.title: Workflow Time Breakdown (P95, per attempt)

panels.description: Step duration percentiles for a single attempt (queue + processing). Step retries land as separate samples — see Step Failures for retry rate. "No step ran in the time range" is shown both when the engines measured nothing here and when no engine reported.

defaults.noValue: No step ran in the time range

panels.title: Step Duration (per attempt)

panels.description: Per-attempt P95 of step queue wait (engine/DB overhead between steps) and active execution, stacked. Stack height is the sum of two marginal P95s — useful for seeing whether queue or processing drives tail latency, but it does not reconcile arithmetically with the Step Duration panel's P95(total) because percentiles are not additive across the queue/processing decomposition. Within a single attempt, queue + processing does equal total by construction. "No step ran in the time range" is shown both when the engines measured nothing here and when no engine reported.

defaults.noValue: No step ran in the time range

panels.title: Step Time Breakdown (P95, per attempt)

panels.description: Rate of step executions by outcome. Nothing counted is a line at 0 where the engines report but have counted nothing here yet.
panels.title: Step Execution

panels.description: Workflows per second taken back from an engine process that stopped renewing its lease, for example one that crashed, so another process can run them, added up over the selected service owners and their engine processes. Engine errors are under Where to look, in Engine Errors by Operation. Nothing counted is a line at 0 where the engines report but have counted nothing here yet.
panels.title: Stale Workflows Reclaimed

panels.description: Npgsql connection pool: idle vs active connections. Stacked area shows total pool usage over time. These are Npgsql's standard db.client.* metrics, which the metric allowlist in Altinn's environments drops (only altinn.*, http.* and signalr.server.* pass), so this row shows data only locally.
panels.title: Pool Utilization

panels.description: Npgsql connection creation time and command execution duration. High create time = network/PG issue. High command duration = slow queries. These are Npgsql's standard db.client.* metrics, which the metric allowlist in Altinn's environments drops (only altinn.*, http.* and signalr.server.* pass), so this row shows data only locally.
panels.title: Latency (P95 / P50)

panels.description: Currently executing commands, total open connections, and pool max boundary. Executing near pool limit = saturation. These are Npgsql's standard db.client.* metrics, which the metric allowlist in Altinn's environments drops (only altinn.*, http.* and signalr.server.* pass), so this row shows data only locally.
panels.title: Connections & Pool Limits

panels.description: Worker concurrency slots: used vs total capacity
panels.title: Worker Slots

panels.description: Database operation concurrency slots: used vs total capacity
panels.title: DB Slots

panels.description: HTTP call concurrency slots: used vs total capacity
panels.title: HTTP Slots

panels.description: Inbox slots: active workflows against the backpressure threshold, used vs total capacity. Both are derived from the database-wide active workflow count, which every replica reports identically, so replicas are combined with max() rather than sum().
panels.title: Inbox Slots

panels.description: Processing loop iterations per minute. Nothing counted is a line at 0 where the engines report but have counted nothing here yet.
panels.title: Main Loop Rate

panels.description: P95 of each main-loop iteration broken down: Queue (post-fetch wait — debounce or ~500ms idle ceiling) and Active Work (fetch + dispatch), stacked. Total is the joint P95 of the same iterations, drawn outside the stack: percentiles are not additive, so it will not equal the stack height, and the gap between them is exactly how much that non-additivity costs you here. For iteration throughput see Main Loop Rate. "No main loop pass was measured in the time range" is shown both when the engines measured nothing here and when no engine reported.

defaults.noValue: No main loop pass was measured in the time range

panels.title: Main Loop Time (P95)

panels.description: Rate of database operations by outcome. Nothing counted is a line at 0 where the engines report but have counted nothing here yet.
panels.title: Database Operations

panels.description: Update buffer throughput: total submitted (deduped + flushed), items flushed to DB, and items eliminated by deduplication. Nothing counted is a line at 0 where the engines report but have counted nothing here yet.
panels.title: Update Buffer Throughput

panels.description: Receive workflows the rendezvous could not answer for — tagged unregistered or undecided. Both mean the engine is violating an invariant of its own rendezvous, which is why they fail the step critically rather than retryably: a retry would launder the violation. ALERT ON ANY VALUE ABOVE ZERO; this is a different pager from a step failing because the app returned an error. The `or vector(0)` keeps the panel reading a true zero rather than “No data” before the counter has ever fired.
panels.title: Rendezvous Violations

panels.description: Mailboxes still open more than one MailboxSweepInterval past their deadline. Exactly zero is the only healthy reading — anything else means the deadline sweep is not running or not draining. A mass timeout can make it briefly non-zero while one tick drains, so alert on persistence rather than on a single sample. The count saturates at 10 000, so never read it as an exact backlog size. Every replica reports the same database-wide count, so replicas are combined with max() rather than sum().
panels.title: Overdue Open Mailboxes

panels.description: Accepted deliveries that no receiver was ever enqueued for, counted when a mailbox closes at its deadline. Not an engine fault — the message was accepted and stored exactly as promised — but it means a saga stopped reading before the other side stopped writing, so the reply was never consumed. Non-zero deserves a look at the owning app, not a page.
panels.title: Unpaired Deliveries

panels.description: Mints and closures per second. Minted excludes idempotent replays, which create nothing. Closures are split by reason: `request` is a DELETE from the owning saga (the healthy path), `deadline` is the sweep closing a mailbox nobody came back for. A `deadline` share that climbs means sagas are abandoning exchanges rather than finishing them. Nothing counted is a line at 0 where the engines report but have counted nothing here yet.
panels.title: Mailbox Lifecycle

panels.description: Every delivery request the engine answered, by verdict. `accepted` appended a message; `duplicate` replayed a stored idempotency key and is a healthy forwarder retrying, not an error. The refusals — `closed`, `not_found`, `log_full`, `too_large`, `invalid` — store nothing, so their keys stay free for a corrected replay. Note that the idempotency lookup runs before the refusals, so a kept message still replays 200 after the mailbox closed. Nothing counted is a line at 0 where the engines report but have counted nothing here yet.
panels.title: Deliveries by Outcome

panels.description: Receive workflows entering and leaving the rendezvous. Every receiver registers, not only the parked ones. Created, by enqueue outcome: `held` is created waiting for a message that has not arrived, `delivered` is created already holding one, `closed` is created against a mailbox that had already closed. Released, by cause: `delivered` is a message arriving for a parked receiver, `closed` is closure releasing every receiver at once. Receivers created `held` and total releases should track each other over time; a persistent gap is receivers that never got woken. Nothing counted is a line at 0 where the engines report but have counted nothing here yet.
panels.title: Receivers: Created & Released

panels.description: Percentiles of the gap between a parked receiver being released and a worker first claiming it. NOTIFY is issued inside the releasing transaction and the processor debounces it by 10ms, so the healthy population is tens of milliseconds; a release whose NOTIFY was missed is claimed on the next fetch cycle, which puts a soft ceiling around the 500ms idle poll. Anything materially above that is worker starvation, not mailbox latency. Values are clamped at zero because the two ends come from two pods' clocks. "No receiver woke in the time range" is shown both when the engines measured nothing here and when no engine reported.

defaults.noValue: No receiver woke in the time range

panels.title: Receiver Wake Latency

panels.description: The one thing the engine emits that answers “is mailbox batching actually happening?” — requests answered by a flush divided by flushes, per operation, over the same window. Both counters are recorded at the same point once a batch is known answered, so a faulted flush counts in neither. 1.0 means every request flushed alone, and for deliveries that is worse than the bespoke path it replaced: the break-even is a mean batch of about 1.25 (the batched delivery flush issues a fixed five statements). The ceiling is MaxBatchSize, 100 for all three buffers; a ratio pinned there means the buffer is saturated and that setting is what to tune next. altinn.workflow_engine.mailbox_buffer.depth cannot answer this question — see the Buffer Depth panel. Nothing counted is a line at 0 where the engines report but have counted nothing here yet.
panels.title: Mean Batch Size (flushed ÷ batches)

panels.description: Mailbox requests waiting for a batch flush, per operation. Read this as LATENCY, not capacity: the queues wait rather than refuse when full, so a sustained depth means callers waiting longer for a verdict, never requests turned away. Read only the sustained value — it is a 5s sample of a queue that fills and drains between flushes, and a storm accepting 3.86 messages per flush held it at zero throughout. A zero here is therefore no evidence the queue never filled, and this panel cannot tell you whether batching is happening. Mean Batch Size is what does.
panels.title: Buffer Depth

panels.description: Rate of in-flight workflows abandoned because the row's lease token no longer matches at write-back. Non-zero indicates heartbeat lag or aggressive maintenance reclaim — workflows self-heal via reclaim, but downstream side effects may have been duplicated. Reads 0 rather than No data while the engine reports and this has not happened.
panels.title: Lease Lost

panels.description: Rate of fetched workflows skipped because they were already in-flight on this host — same-host DbMaintenance reclaim raced the main fetch loop. Self-heals on the next maintenance sweep. Reads 0 rather than No data while the engine reports and this has not happened.
panels.title: Fetch Race Dropped

panels.description: Rate of fire-and-forget status updates dropped because the update-buffer channel was full. These are real losses (intermediate progress updates) — non-zero signals backpressure exceeding the buffer's capacity. Reads 0 rather than No data while the engine reports and this has not happened.
panels.title: Update Buffer Dropped

panels.description: Operator actions on workflows the engine had already placed, in the last 5 minutes. Discrete and rare, so a count over the window rather than a per-second rate. Nudged cleared a parked workflow's backoff so it runs on the next fetch cycle instead of when its timer elapses — the engine's push channel, an acceleration that is never load-bearing for correctness. Abandoned wrote off an unsuccessful terminal workflow, which stops it condemning dependents evaluated afterwards and atomically releases its enqueue idempotency key, so replaying the same fingerprint creates a fresh workflow instead of deduplicating onto the write-off. Nothing counted is a line at 0 where the engines report but have counted nothing here yet.
panels.title: Operator Interventions

panels.description: DependencyFailed workflows re-enqueued in the last 5 minutes because their dependencies have all completed since — the engine healing itself, and the only counter on this row nobody triggered by hand. The maintenance sweep that does it runs once a minute, so this lags its cause. On its own panel rather than beside the interventions because abandonments outrun recoveries by two orders of magnitude and would flatten this to the baseline. Nothing counted is a line at 0 where the engines report but have counted nothing here yet.
panels.title: Dependency Recovery
